title: Ratio Instinct
subject: math
tagline: Feel proportions before you calculate them.

lessons.title: Parts of a whole
lessons.summary: See a ratio as a relationship, not two lonely numbers.

steps.title: A ratio is a relationship
steps.body: When a recipe says 2 cups flour to 1 cup water, you are not memorizing two amounts. You are locking a relationship: flour is twice the water — no matter how big the batch gets.
steps.callout: Think: for every 1 of this, how many of that?

steps.prompt: A paint mix uses 3 parts blue to 1 part white. If you use 2 cups of white, how much blue do you need to keep the same color?
steps.hint: White doubled from 1 to 2. Blue must double too.
steps.success: Yes — 3:1 scales to 6:2. Same color, bigger batch.

steps.prompt: Which pairs describe the same ratio as 2:3?
steps.hint: Scale both sides by the same number. Order matters — 3:2 is flipped.

steps.prompt: Arrange these juice mixes from weakest to strongest (least concentrate to most).
steps.hint: More water relative to concentrate means a weaker drink.
steps.success: Less water per part concentrate → stronger flavor.

lessons.title: Scale sense
lessons.summary: Resize a scene without breaking the relationship.

steps.title: Scaling keeps the shape of the relationship
steps.body: If every quantity multiplies by the same factor, the ratio stays put. That is why maps, recipes, and screen layouts can grow or shrink and still feel right.

steps.prompt: A map scale is 1 cm : 5 km. A road measures 4 cm on the map. How many kilometers is the real road?
steps.hint: Each centimeter stands for 5 km. Multiply.
steps.success: 4 × 5 = 20 km. The ratio did the conversion for you.

steps.prompt: Match each scene to the ratio it describes.

pairs.left: Five wins out of eight games

steps.hint: Write left:right in the order the scene mentions.
steps.success: You are reading ratios out of everyday language.
